summary: Specifies the frame format and MTU for sending IPv6 packets over FDDI networks, including handling of bridges to other media. It was replaced by RFC 2467.

eli5.summary: This explains how to put new-style internet packets onto an old fiber ring network so they fit properly.

questions: how does fddi work with ipv6
subtitle: How to send new-style internet packets over fiber ring networks.

tldr.problem: IPv6 was new and the internet needed rules for transmitting IPv6 packets over existing FDDI networks, which have different MTU sizes and frame formats than Ethernet.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2019 defines a 4352-octet MTU, frame format using LLC/SNAP encapsulation, and rules for bridges that connect FDDI to other media, including an adjacency detection scheme.
tldr.outcome: IPv6 could run reliably on FDDI networks, but this RFC was replaced by RFC 2467 which provides more comprehensive guidance.

today: RFC 2019 was a Proposed Standard and has been obsoleted by RFC 2467, which provides updated specifications for IPv6 transmission over FDDI networks.

sections.title: Introduction and Overview
sections.content:
RFC 2019 specifies how to transmit IPv6 packets over FDDI networks. FDDI (Fiber Distributed Data Interface) was a high-speed ring-shaped local-area network technology common in the 1990s, with a maximum frame size of 4500 octets. The RFC defines the MTU (maximum transmission unit) that IPv6 packets can use, the frame format in which they are wrapped, how link-local addresses are formed, and how IPv6 works when FDDI networks are bridged to other media such as Ethernet.

The memo also specifies the method of forming IPv6 link-local addresses on FDDI networks and the content of source and target link-layer address options used in neighbor discovery messages.
sections.eli5: FDDI is an old fiber-optic ring network. This document explains how to put IPv6 internet packets on those rings, including how to handle them when the ring is connected to other network types.

sections.title: Frame Format and MTU
sections.content:
FDDI permits frame lengths of 4500 octets including at least 22 octets of data-link encapsulation. Subtracting 8 octets of LLC/SNAP header leaves room for IPv6 packets of up to 4470 octets. However, to allow for future extensions and variable sizes in the MAC header and frame status fields, the default MTU for IPv6 packets on FDDI is set to 4352 octets. This size may be reduced through router advertisements containing an MTU option or by manual configuration on each node.

IPv6 packets are transmitted in LLC/SNAP frames using long-format 48-bit addresses. The frame contains a Frame Code (FC) field indicating the priority and asynchronous/synchronous transmission type, followed by destination and source FDDI addresses, an LLC/SNAP header with DSAP and SSAP set to 0xAA, a control field set to 0x03, an OUI of 000000, and an Ethertype of 0x86DD, followed by the IPv6 header and payload.
sections.eli5: Each message on FDDI has a specific structure with a header showing priority, addresses, and type information, then the actual data. The biggest message can be 4352 bytes, which leaves room for the wrapper and the actual packet.

sections.title: Interaction with Bridges
sections.content:
When FDDI networks are connected to other media through 802.1d MAC bridges (such as bridges between FDDI and Ethernet), the situation becomes complex. Many bridges do not support IPv4 Path MTU discovery correctly, and IPv6 should not depend on bridge support for packet fragmentation.

For correct operation in mixed-media bridged networks, the smallest MTU of all media must be advertised by routers in an MTU option. If no routers are present, each node connected to a medium with larger default MTU must be manually configured with the smaller MTU. To help nodes detect when they can send larger unicast packets directly to FDDI neighbors without going through bridges, RFC 2019 specifies a simple FDDI adjacency detection mechanism. Nodes implementing this mechanism set a non-zero LLC priority in neighbor discovery frames transmitted on FDDI. A node that receives a neighbor discovery frame with non-zero priority from another node may send unicast IPv6 packets up to the full 4352-octet FDDI MTU to that node, regardless of any smaller MTU configured elsewhere.
sections.eli5: When FDDI rings are connected to other networks through bridges, routers or administrators need to tell nodes what size packets are safe. There is a smart trick: nodes can tell if a neighbor is directly on the FDDI ring (and can handle big packets) by looking at a priority bit in special messages.

sections.title: Link-Local Addresses and Address Mapping
sections.content:
IPv6 link-local addresses on FDDI networks are formed by appending the interface's IEEE 802 address to the 80-bit prefix FE80::. The address token used for stateless autoconfiguration is the interface's built-in 48-bit IEEE 802 address in canonical bit order, as it would appear in an Ethernet frame header. An IPv6 address prefix used for stateless autoconfiguration must be 80 bits in length, leaving 48 bits for the interface identifier.

For unicast address mapping, when the link layer is FDDI, the Source/Target Link-layer Address option in neighbor discovery messages contains the 48-bit FDDI IEEE 802 address in canonical bit order. For multicast, an IPv6 packet with a multicast destination address is transmitted to an FDDI multicast address whose first two octets are 0x3333 hexadecimal and whose last four octets are the last four octets of the IPv6 multicast address.
sections.eli5: Every FDDI interface has a unique 48-bit hardware address. IPv6 link-local addresses are formed by combining the prefix FE80:: with that hardware address. For multicast (broadcasts to multiple receivers), the IPv6 address is mapped to an FDDI multicast address starting with 0x3333.

sections.title: Summary
sections.content: RFC 2019 provides the specification needed to run IPv6 over FDDI networks, a key capability when FDDI was still widely deployed in enterprise networks. The RFC is now obsoleted by RFC 2467, which provides enhanced specifications and additional methods for transmission of IPv6 packets over FDDI networks, but the fundamental principles described here—the 4352-octet MTU, the LLC/SNAP frame format, the adjacency detection scheme, and the address mapping rules—remain important for understanding how IPv6 was adapted to work on FDDI hardware.
sections.eli5: This RFC was the rulebook for IPv6 on FDDI rings. It has been replaced by a newer version with more details, but the core ideas are still there: standard packet sizes, a format for wrapping packets, a way to detect direct neighbors, and rules for turning IPv6 addresses into hardware addresses.
